When does asking AI to revise its answer help?

Mudit Gurnani · November 16, 2026 · 200 task families · 600 answers

Data and methods ↓ · Chart data ↓ · Research code: publication pending
body:
A better prompt, or a second look?

When an AI gives an answer, there are two easy ways to ask for more care. Add a checklist before it responds, or ask it to review the answer it has already written. Both sound sensible. Neither tells us whether the final answer will actually be better.

We tested these two changes with Luna on hard coding problems and planning puzzles. A structured prompt did not demonstrate an improvement over a simple request. One revision did help on the coding tasks: success rose from 59% to 69%. The planning result was less clear.

The useful distinction is between changing an answer and improving it. A revision can repair a mistake, preserve a correct answer, or break something that already worked. We measured all three.

Earlier work has found both benefits from iterative refinement and failures of self-correction without external feedback. Our test asks a narrower question about one revision in one fixed setup. How this relates to prior research →

Three ways to solve the same task

The experiment used 200 task families: 100 coding problems labeled VERY_HARD, 50 graph-coloring puzzles and 50 Sokoban puzzles. Graph coloring asks for an assignment that gives connected vertices different colors. Sokoban asks for a sequence of moves that pushes boxes onto targets.

A · ONE CALL

Just solve it

A simple request to solve the task and return the required answer.

S · ONE CALL

Use a checklist

Check requirements, choose an approach and consider constraints before answering.

R · TWO CALLS IN TOTAL

Review that answer

Take the exact S answer and revise it once. Retain it if it is already correct.

Every task received a simple answer (A), a structured answer (S), and a revision of S (R). The revision received the original task and the exact saved S response. It did not receive a test result, a correctness label or a hint about what went wrong. We also revised empty and malformed S responses rather than dropping them.

All three used the same model setting: openai/gpt-6-luna, medium reasoning and a 16,384 output-token ceiling. The simple prompt still used that reasoning setting; “simple” refers to the instructions, not to an absence of model reasoning.

We saved all 600 answers before grading any of them. A coding answer had to pass the stored tests under the fixed execution limits. Planning answers had to satisfy their task constraints. We always scored the revised answer, rather than choosing whichever of S or R looked better. Task selection and grading details →

Coding gained ten correct answers

The coding result was unusually clean in this sample. Revision fixed 10 of the 41 answers that S had failed and preserved all 59 that S had passed. The remaining 31 still failed. That produced a 10 percentage-point gain.

The structured prompt alone did not help on average: it scored 59/100, compared with 60/100 for the simple prompt. Underneath that one-answer difference, it gained 10 correct answers and lost 11. Adding a checklist changed which problems were solved without establishing a net improvement.

The revision result passed our planned statistical rule even after correcting for all four comparisons. Its pointwise 95% interval was +5 to +16 percentage points, with an adjusted p-value of 0.0078. “No regressions” describes these 100 coding tasks. It is not a guarantee that revision will never break a correct answer. Exact tests, intervals and decision rule →

Planning improved, but also regressed

Planning success rose from 60% with a simple prompt to 66% with structure and 74% after revision. Those are promising observed differences. They did not pass the planned statistical test after correction for multiple comparisons.

Revision fixed 18 planning answers but broke 10 that had been correct. The net gain was eight answers, with a pointwise interval from −2 to +18 percentage points. The data are compatible with a small loss as well as a useful gain.

The puzzle types also behaved differently. Graph coloring rose from 45/50 after structure to 50/50 after revision, with five fixes and no regressions. Sokoban rose from 21/50 to 24/50, but that small net gain hid 13 fixes and 10 regressions. These subtype results are descriptive, not additional confirmatory wins. All puzzle-type results →

This is why we would not summarize the study as “self-correction works.” The coding result supports a specific workflow on this bank. The planning result reminds us that another attempt can also undo correct work.

What did the extra call cost?

Revision costs an extra call for every task. The revised totals include both the first answer and its revision.

Model cost per successful task is the total cost of all 100 tasks, including failed answers, divided by the number that passed. Revision produced more correct answers but cost more per success in both domains. Only the coding improvement met our statistical rule.

We did not test whether giving the first attempt more reasoning time, or asking for a fresh answer, would help as much as revision. We cannot say which option gives the most improvement for the same budget.

The first answers are already included in the revised totals. Adding the structured and revised rows together would count those first answers twice.

These are observed model charges, not forecasts. They exclude infrastructure and an unresolved charge from one interrupted request, so the full experiment bill remains unknown. Costs, token counts and missing measurements →

What we learned

For this coding bank and Luna configuration, one neutral revision is worth considering when another call is acceptable. We found a measurable gain over the structured first answer, without an observed coding regression. We found no comparable evidence that the structured prompt alone improves on the simple one.

For planning, the result is unresolved. The aggregate rate rose, but revisions both repaired and damaged answers. A policy that always accepts the latest answer needs to account for both.

The next decision should depend on the task and the cost of a wrong answer, not on a general rule to ask every model to “think again.” This study supports a bounded coding result. It does not establish a universal prompting recipe, an equal-compute advantage, or a substitute for checking the final answer.

We chose Luna and these types of tasks after preliminary testing, then fixed the task list before collecting the answers. The results may not represent other problems. The coding problems are public, so we cannot rule out that Luna encountered them during training. We tried each workflow once per task, always in the same order. One interrupted request was replaced after approval, but its original outcome and charge remain unknown. These limits mean we should be cautious about expecting the same results elsewhere. What these results cannot establish →

Appendix

Methods, detailed results and study limitations. Expand a section to read more.

Tasks, prompts and grading

There were 200 fixed families, each with A/S/R endpoints: 100 VERY_HARD coding problems, 50 graph-coloring and 50 Sokoban puzzles. The coding bank contained 55 train-split and 45 test-split TACO tasks, with 95 from an older cohort and five recent reserves. Planning combined 84 newly qualified tasks and 16 saved qualified tasks. These source split names do not establish absence from model training.

A asked the model to solve the task in the required format. Coding S added requirements, approach, boundary-case and implementation checks. Planning S added constraint, complete-solution and final-state checks. The revision instruction was:

Review your previous answer against the original task and requirements. It may already be correct. Correct any errors you identify; otherwise retain it. Return one complete final answer in the same required format.

The saved visible S response was passed exactly, even when empty or malformed. R received no grading feedback. All endpoints used medium reasoning and a 16,384 output-token limit. Tasks followed the accepted bank order, with A, S and R consecutive. We sampled one trajectory per family and froze all 600 answers before grading. No best-of-S/R selection, task refill or outcome-based exclusion was used.

Coding required all stored tests to pass under pinned software, container image and limits. Planning used the accepted deterministic constraint verifiers. Resolved invalid or truncated endpoints counted as failures. All 600 grades resolved; independent raw-result and final-report audits accepted the saved evidence. The source records and finite stored tests do not establish correctness for every possible input.

Paired comparisons and uncertainty

The four primary contrasts were S−A and R−S within coding and within planning. Each paired comparison used the same 100 families. We used two-sided exact McNemar tests, Holm correction over four tests, and required a positive effect with adjusted p ≤ 0.05 for formal improvement. R−A was not a primary contrast.

Intervals are percentile pointwise 95% intervals from 20,000 paired family-bootstrap draws, seed 20261111, using linear-interpolated quantiles. Planning resamples preserved 50 graph-coloring and 50 Sokoban tasks. These are not simultaneous 95% intervals. Family independence and bootstrap approximation remain assumptions. A non-significant comparison does not establish equivalence.

Cost, tokens and missing data

The 600 settled endpoint calls cost $1.466287055 and recorded 355,984 input and 2,858,780 output tokens, totaling 3,214,764. Output includes reasoning tokens; cache detail columns must not be added to total tokens. Including the unresolved original request, the current campaign made 601 physical requests for 600 logical endpoints, so its complete charge and token totals remain unknown.

For 100 coding endpoints, standalone A cost $0.281233425, S $0.285268650, and R (S+R) $0.451084430. For 100 planning endpoints, the corresponding charges were $0.288379500, $0.272989000 and $0.445589700. The standalone tables overlap and must not be summed as experiment spend. Coding A additionally has the orphan request, so its full operational cost is unknown.

Earlier history adds 397 physical requests and 396 logical endpoints. Lifetime totals are 998 physical requests, 996 logical endpoints and $3.768408305 in known API charges, with two unresolved charges. Their reserves total $12.411352800. The $10 infrastructure commitment is not an invoice or measured spending. Full API and all-in actual costs remain unknown.

Full guarded grading wall time was 11,044.133 seconds. Generation and whole-campaign wall times remain unknown. The replacement’s logical duration is unknown; its measured physical duration was 101.400575666 seconds. Historical missing durations remain unknown. Summed request durations are not wall time or time-to-correct-answer. The downloadable data includes metric-level known sums and missing counts.

Scope, interruption and limits

The model/domain scope was chosen after earlier calibration. This is a fixed-bank comparison, not evidence that calibration headroom predicts workflow gains. Public coding sources may be present in training, and finite family exclusions do not prove uncontamination. The older coding cohort and authored planning tasks limit generalization; the reported coding result is not an official TACO benchmark score.

One sampled trajectory per family and fixed A/S/R ordering leave stochastic, service-time and provider-alias variation unresolved. R uses more compute than S. We did not compare revision with a matched-budget first attempt, an independent second attempt, or a larger model. Passing stored tests is a finite correctness result, not proof of general program correctness. Perfect graph-coloring performance in 50 selected tasks is not general planning mastery.

The original run stopped after a connection reset, leaving 279 accepted answers and one request with unknown remote completion and charge. The owner explicitly approved preserving the saved responses, making one replacement with the exact same wire body, and completing the remaining 320 untouched slots. Provider lookup was incomplete and recovery was not exhausted. The original charge remains unknown. This is completion under that amendment, not under the original no-retry protocol. The interruption and replacement add time/provider variation; an identical request body does not guarantee an identical response.

No additional retry, replacement, prompt optimization, answer selection, regrading or new study was used to obtain these results. Statistical uncertainty remains substantial outside the coding revision contrast.

Related research

Madaan et al., Self-Refine (2023) studies iterative feedback and refinement by the same model across seven tasks. It reports improvements over one-step generation. Our setup uses a single neutral revision, a different model and task bank, and no separate feedback-generation loop. It is not a direct replication.

Huang et al., Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024) examines intrinsic self-correction without external feedback and reports difficulty, including degraded performance in some settings. Our mixed coding and planning results reinforce the need to specify model, task and revision procedure; they do not settle the broader question.
